name: Leader Election
intent: Let a group of machines agree on exactly one of them to act as the leader, and choose a new one automatically when the leader fails, without ever ending up with two leaders.
scenario: A database cluster has five nodes. One must accept writes and tell the others what to do. When that node crashes at 3 a.m., the cluster must pick a replacement by itself, and must never let two nodes both believe they are in charge.
problem: Many systems need a single decision maker: the primary database, the scheduler, the owner of a shard. A fixed leader is a single point of failure, but picking a new one carelessly causes split brain: two leaders accept conflicting writes, and the data is corrupted. Nodes also cannot tell a crashed leader from a slow network.

howItWorks.title: The leader sends regular heartbeats
howItWorks.text: While it is healthy, the leader tells all followers 'I am still here' every few hundred milliseconds. Each follower resets a timer every time it hears one. Followers do not need to ask who the leader is: silence is the signal.

howItWorks.title: A follower whose timer expires becomes a candidate
howItWorks.text: If no heartbeat arrives before the election timeout, a follower assumes the leader is gone. It increases its term (a number that counts elections), votes for itself and asks the others to vote for it. Timeouts are randomised so that usually one node times out first and wins, rather than all of them splitting the vote.

howItWorks.title: A majority decides
howItWorks.text: Each node votes for at most one candidate per term. A candidate becomes leader only when a strict majority of the whole cluster (3 of 5) votes for it. Two majorities always overlap, so two leaders cannot be elected in the same term.

howItWorks.title: Terms keep old leaders out
howItWorks.text: Every message carries its sender's term. A node that sees a higher term updates itself and steps down if it was a leader. So when a network partition heals, the old leader meets the new term and immediately becomes a follower.

howItWorks.title: Use a proven implementation
howItWorks.text: Raft, Paxos and ZooKeeper-style coordination services implement this correctly, including awkward cases like split votes and a leader cut off from the majority. Most applications should take a lock or lease from such a service instead of writing their own election.

pros: A single leader keeps decisions simple and writes ordered
Well-understood algorithms and ready-made libraries exist
cons: Needs a majority: a 5-node cluster tolerates 2 failures, and a minority partition cannot elect
Failover takes time, during which there is no leader and writes wait
A slow network or a long garbage-collection pause looks like a crash and triggers needless elections
The leader is still a bottleneck for all writes
whenToUse: Replicated databases and coordination services that need one primary
Singleton jobs such as schedulers and cron runners across several instances
Assigning the owner of each partition or shard
whenNotToUse: Workloads that can be spread across all nodes with no coordination
Hand-writing your own election instead of using a proven library or service
pitfalls: Even-sized clusters, which give no extra fault tolerance and can tie
A leader that keeps acting after it has lost the majority (use leases and fencing tokens)
Election timeouts shorter than ordinary network or pause delays, causing constant re-elections
Trusting wall-clock time instead of terms to decide who is the newest leader
